description_full: Smithfield Foods, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, produces various packaged meats and fresh pork products in the United States and internationally. It operates through Packaged Meats, Fresh Pork, Hog Production, and Other segments. The Packaged Meats segment processes fresh meat into various packaged meats products, including bacon, sausage, hot dogs, deli and lunch meats, dry sausage products, ham products, ready-to-eat products, and prepared foods to retail and foodservice customers. This segment markets its packaged meat products under the Smithfield, Eckrich, Nathan's Famous, Farmland, Armour, Farmer John, Kretschmar, Krakus, John Morrell, Cook's, Gwaltney, Carando, Margherita, Curly's and Smithfield Culinary, as well as under private labels. The Fresh Pork segment processes live hogs into a variety of primal, sub-primal, and offal products, such as bellies, butts, hams, loins, trimmings, picnics, and ribs. This segment sells its fresh pork products to retail, foodservice and industrial customers, as well as to export markets, including China, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, and Canada. The Hog Production segment produces and raises its hogs on various company-owned farms and farms that are owned and operated by contract farmers. This segment also sells livestock feed and grains; and provides transportation and other ancillary services. The Other segment engages in the bioscience operations uses raw materials from hogs that process to manufacture heparin products, including an active pharmaceutical ingredient that mitigates the risk of blood clots; and produces fresh pork products in Mexico. The company was founded in 1936 and is headquartered in Smithfield, Virginia. Smithfield Foods, Inc. is a subsidiary of SFDS UK Holdings Limited.

financial_summary: Smithfield Foods, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer defensive business with a $7.6B market cap on $15.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 11% against a 7% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 12% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $718M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.07× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 32× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 88% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.

With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.62, it is more defensive than the market.

Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 9.4% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 14.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $22.79 on average, 18% above the price.
The price implies 5.5% annual cash-flow growth.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.23).
It runs a 12% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.07x.
ROE of 15% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.4% of revenue on R&D.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA ($1.3B of cash against $2.0B of debt), with interest covered 31.5x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.2, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.1% over 3 years and 0.7% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 93% of profits supports about 9.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 2.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 9.2% on average.
Analysts expect 1.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 88.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 15%.
It returns 2.1% a year to shareholders (6.5% in dividends, less 3.1% of net share issuance).
Short interest is elevated at 12.7% of the float, 2.8 days to cover.
people: With about 33,500 employees, each generates about $464K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Defensive median.
That works out to $21K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $9.8M (21x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
